query: Accrued unbilled rev. impacts rev. recog. & op. perf.
final_answer: Accrued unbilled revenue represents revenue that has been earned by delivering goods or services but has not yet been billed to the customer. This occurs due to timing differences between when a company performs its obligations under a contract and when it is able to issue an invoice. Impact on Revenue Recognition: - Revenue is recognized when performance obligations are satisfied (i.e., when goods or services have been delivered), even if the billing has not yet occurred. Accrued unbilled revenue is recorded as an asset on the balance sheet to reflect this earned but not yet billed revenue (Chunks 1, 4, 6, 10, 14). - For example, Dominion Energy and Virginia Power include significant amounts of accrued unbilled revenue in their customer receivables based on estimated electricity and gas delivered but not yet billed (Chunks 1, 4). Impact on Operating Performance: - Accrued unbilled revenue can enhance reported revenue and operating performance metrics, as it ensures that all earned revenue is recognized in the period when the service is provided or the product is delivered, regardless of billing cycle (Chunks 1, 4, 10). - However, since cash has not yet been collected for unbilled revenue, it may not immediately impact cash flow, and higher balances of unbilled revenue could indicate longer billing cycles or delays in invoicing (Chunk 10). - The presence of accrued unbilled revenue helps provide a more accurate picture of a company’s operating activity during a period, aligning revenue recognition with service delivery or product transfer (Chunks 1, 4, 10). In summary, accrued unbilled revenue ensures revenue recognition matches actual performance, which is important for accurately reporting operating results, even if billing and cash collection occur later.

query: Revenue recognition: principal vs. agent criteria?
final_answer: The principal vs. agent criteria for revenue recognition involve determining whether a company controls a specified good or service before it is transferred to the customer (principal) or arranges for another party to provide the good or service (agent). Key indicators and considerations include: - Whether the company is primarily responsible for fulfilling the promise to provide the specified goods or services. - Whether the company has inventory risk before the good or service is transferred to the customer. - Whether the company has discretion in establishing the price for the specified good or service. If the evaluation indicates the company controls the good or service prior to transfer, it acts as a principal and recognizes revenue on a gross basis (i.e., total sales price to the customer). If not, the company acts as an agent and recognizes revenue on a net basis (i.e., only the fee or commission received) (Chunks 1, 2, 3, 4). This assessment is made for each identified performance obligation in a transaction, and requires consideration of contract terms, responsibilities, risks, and pricing authority.

The costs of coupons (as well as other promotional activities) are netted against sales in the period the related sale occurs, reducing reported revenue and therefore impacting the profit and loss (P&L) statement immediately (Chunks 1, 2, 4). If actual coupon redemptions differ from the estimated rates used to establish reserves, the following impacts occur: - On the P&L: - If actual redemptions are higher than estimated, additional expense is recognized in a future period to increase reserves, further reducing net sales and profit in that period. - If actual redemptions are lower than estimated, the excess reserve is reversed, increasing net sales and profit in the period of adjustment. - On cash flow: - Cash flow is affected when coupons are actually redeemed and paid out, not when the reserve is initially established. Since the reserve is a non-cash accounting entry, changes in the reserve estimation affect net income but must be adjusted for in the reconciliation from net income to operating cash flow. If actual redemptions are lower or higher than expected, cash outflows for coupon redemptions will likewise be lower or higher, but the timing may differ from when the expense hits the P&L. As an example, a 0.1% deviation in coupon redemption rates would result in a $0.7 million difference in the reserve requirement (Chunk 2, 4). Such adjustments could materially impact both reported earnings and cash flows from operations. In summary: - The coupon reserve method directly reduces reported revenue and profit when sales occur. - Variances between estimated and actual redemptions lead to future P&L adjustments. - Cash flow is only affected when coupons are redeemed, so reserve changes are non-cash and adjusted for in operating cash flow calculations.

query: Control transfer timing, shipping terms, and carrier, global.
final_answer: The timing of control transfer in global shipping transactions depends on the specific shipping terms agreed upon in the contract, such as FOB (Free On Board) Shipping Point or other Incoterms. Generally: - For FOB Shipping Point (or equivalent terms), control transfers to the customer at the time of shipment. The customer obtains control, and revenue is recognized by the seller when the goods are shipped, as the customer assumes risks and rewards of ownership and the seller has a present right to payment (see DHR.pdf, ALB.pdf, FMC.pdf). - For delivery terms other than FOB Shipping Point, control may transfer upon delivery to the customer’s destination or at another specified point, depending on the contract’s shipping terms and when risks and title pass to the customer (see DHR.pdf, ALB.pdf, ADI.pdf, FMC.pdf). - When shipping and handling activities occur after control has transferred, these are generally considered fulfillment activities, not separate performance obligations, and their costs are accrued when revenue is recognized (see FMC.pdf, BALL.pdf, ALB.pdf). - In logistics and transportation management services, control is considered transferred over the period the shipment is in transit, and revenue is recognized as this service is performed. The company serving as the principal in the transaction (i.e., controlling the service, selecting the carrier, and setting prices) recognizes revenue on a gross basis, while acting as an agent (not controlling the service) results in net revenue recognition (see UBER.pdf, JBHT.pdf). - The use of third-party (independent) carriers is common, especially in global logistics operations, and the entity responsible for arranging the shipment (the principal) selects and contracts with carriers, retains pricing discretion, and is responsible for payment to carriers regardless of the customer’s payment status (see UBER.pdf, JBHT.pdf). In summary, for global shipments, the transfer of control and corresponding revenue recognition occur either at shipment or delivery, depending on the agreed shipping terms and when the customer obtains the significant risks and rewards of ownership. The party arranging the shipment (seller or logistics provider) may use independent carriers, and the principal/agent relationship in the transaction affects how revenue is recognized.
